title: Easy, Difficult and Slow to Warm Up
text:
In 1956, the psychiatrists Alexander Thomas and Stella Chess, a married couple, began the New York Longitudinal Study with their colleague Herbert Birch. At a time when many experts blamed children's problems mainly on their mothers, they wanted to see whether babies came into the world with their own behavioral styles.

They followed 133 children from mostly middle-class New York families, starting in the first months of life. Through detailed interviews with parents about everyday situations, such as baths, feeding, new foods and strangers, they rated each child on nine features, including activity level, regularity of sleep and hunger, reaction to new things, adaptability, intensity and mood.

The ratings clustered into recognizable types. About 40 percent of the children were easy: regular, positive and adaptable. About 10 percent were difficult: irregular, intense and often negative in response to change. About 15 percent were slow to warm up: cautious at first but eventually adapting. The rest were mixed.

Difficult children were more likely to develop behavior problems later, but not inevitably. What mattered, the researchers argued, was the goodness of fit between a child's temperament and the demands and style of the parents. A patient, consistent parent could guide a difficult child well.
lesson: Children arrive with their own temperaments. Instead of fighting a child's nature, adjust your approach so that it fits the child you actually have.
people: Alexander Thomas, Stella Chess, Herbert Birch
source: Thomas, A., Chess, S., and Birch, H. G. (1968). Temperament and Behavior Disorders in Children. New York: New York University Press.
